transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-31
Time: 10:00 AM PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lina Cho (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (Rivermark VP Eng), Aisha Khan (Rivermark Platform Lead), Tom Wu (Rivermark SRE)
Shared artifacts: updated-benchmarks.xlsx (Google Drive), kernel-sweep-notes.md (link), streaming-demo-recording.mp4 (link)

00:00 Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check, audio ok?
00:05 Mark: yeah good here, thanks Samir.
00:12 Samir: cool, agenda - quick run through TTFT numbers from last week, streaming chunking results, sequence length impacts, then Lina will talk kernel choices and proposed sweep, and we finish with next steps.
00:30 Aisha: sounds good. we're still hoping to get TTFT under 120 ms for simple prompts, anything that helps there is high priority.
00:40 Lina: ok quick summary - ran the streaming chunking change we discussed; for typical 300-token responses we see TTFT down from ~160ms to ~140ms on hosted infra, and when we enable chunked streaming with 64-token chunks we saw the first token at ~130ms average, so improvement but not quite 120 yet. there was variability with seq len and batch size.
01:15 Tom: is that on the same model variant as before, the 13B quantized one?
01:20 Lina: yes, same model, 13b quant, using our 4-bit profile. note transcription: sometimes the runtime reports as "Redwood dedicate" in logs, but it's our hosted pool.
01:35 Mark: any difference when we move to dedicated nodes? we saw some jitter on shared hosts.
01:40 Lina: dedicated helps with JIT warmup and less noisy neighbors; last week on a dedicated 8xA100 pool TTFT was more stable and median shifted to ~125ms. so dedicated + streaming is closer to your 120 goal.
02:00 Samir: couple tradeoffs - dedicated reduces latency variance but has cost implications; I put cost delta in the sheet.
02:15 Mark: got it. what's the biggest remaining blocker to hitting 120ms? is it kernel choices, sequence length, or our request pattern?
02:25 Lina: it's a combo. our profiling shows two main factors: kernel selection for attention and the initial token dispatch path. for short prompts, kernel matters less, but for warmup and long seqs the fused-attn kernels give better throughput and slightly better first-token wall time. however, fused-attn has larger memory working set which can affect large-batch scenarios.
03:00 Aisha: can you explain the "dispatch path" - is that the time in the gateway or inside the model runtime?
03:07 Lina: mostly inside the runtime - we have a small dispatch latency where the request is de-serialized, prefixes checked against KV cache, and the first forward kernel enqueued. streaming reduces work before first token by sending early chunks but also add scheduling overhead. sometimes the K V cache hits reduce compute but add lookup time; it's a balancing act.
03:40 Tom: we do have some infra limits - our network team caps some persistent connections and we've seen occasional TLS renegotiation causing spikes. I can work with them to increase keepalive.
03:52 Samir: great - that will help.
04:00 Lina: on kernels: we compared fused-attn vs gemm-backed matmul paths. at seq=512 fused-attn improved steady-state by ~8% and TTFT by ~5% on average. at seq=2048 the gap widens to ~15% steady-state. but gemm path had more consistent memory usage.
04:30 Mark: any quantization impact? currently we're on 4-bit but if we move to 8-bit would TTFT improve?
04:36 Lina: tradeoff - 8-bit can reduce compute slightly but often increases memory bandwidth; sometimes TTFT improves a bit but cost goes up. our recommendation: keep 4-bit for cost, optimize kernels.
05:00 Samir: we ran a micro-benchmark where we disabled continuous batching for a subset and the TTFT improved for small requests by ~10% but throughput dropped under load. so for production we recommend a mix: small routing for low-latency tier and batching for high-throughput background jobs.
05:30 Mark: that could work. how hard is it to set a route policy? Aisha: we would want to route customer-facing requests to low-latency pool.
05:40 Samir: totally doable - we can set policy by route and model pinned. we can also set automatic fallback to cheaper model for non-critical paths.
05:55 Lina: next technical piece - kernel sweep. I'll run fused-attn vs gemm vs the newer "stream-optimized" kernels we forked in last quarter. I'll sweep across seq len 256/512/1024/2048 and batch sizes 1,2,4 and collect median+95p TTFT.
06:20 Mark: please include streaming chunk sizes 32/64/128 in that sweep.
06:25 Lina: yes will do.
06:30 Aisha: timeline?
06:32 Lina: aiming to have initial plots by 2027-04-05. I'll post to the bench sheet and share a short summary.
06:40 Tom: for the sample workload - we'll upload 100 representative requests that mirror our traffic, varying prompt length and context. we'll also tag them for high-priority routes.
06:50 Samir: perfect. I'll add a TTFT row to the bench sheet and include cost per 1M tokens for each config so you can see economics.
07:05 Mark: curious about streaming chunking artifacts - do we see coherence issues or more partial responses?
07:12 Lina: minor, mainly in generation order. streaming can increase chances of partial tokenization artifacts if client isn't handling chunk boundaries carefully; our SDK handles it but if you have a custom client there might be edge cases.
07:35 Aisha: security note - we're going to need SOC2 scoping and an on-prem option in the future; for now VPC peering and SSO with SAML are must-haves.
07:50 Samir: we have SAML SSO and VPC options; private deployments are available but will add to timeline. I'll attach our security pack in the follow-up.
08:02 Mark: will you include audit log retention options in that pack? that's a requirement.
08:07 Samir: yes.
08:10 Lina: one more datapoint - we tried reducing prefix KV lookups for some request types and that shaved ~6-8ms off TTFT on average for short prompts. if you can annotate requests that don't need full KV checks we can route them through a faster path.
08:30 Tom: we can do that; our router can add a header indicating minimal context.
08:35 Samir: great - that could be low-hanging fruit.
08:40 Mark: any callouts on monitoring? how will we observe TTFT in prod?
08:45 Lina: Console already emits token-level breakdown and per-route latency. we'll add TTFT metric and a dashboard per model and route for you.
09:00 Samir: ok let's do a quick recap and next steps. Recap: streaming chunking and dedicated nodes are the two biggest levers; kernel sweep to quantify; customer to upload request samples; security docs to be shared; cost delta in bench sheet.
09:25 Aisha: agreed.
09:30 Mark: timeline works, we'll aim to get samples by 4/5.
09:35 Samir: perfect. I'll send updated bench sheet and the security pack after this call. Lina will post kernel sweep results by 4/5. Tom will share infra constraints by 4/2. Mark will upload samples by 4/5.
09:50 Samir: any final questions?
09:55 Mark: none from me, thanks.
09:58 Aisha: thanks everyone.
10:00 Samir: thanks all, talk next week.

Meeting close.

Notes about transcription quality: occasional mis-hearings ("Redwood dedicate" for "Redwood Dedicated", "K V cache" tokenization), speaker overlaps in a couple of spots.
